summary: Defines how chunk flags in the Stream Control Transmission Protocol (SCTP) are registered with IANA, and creates a registry for the flags of currently defined chunk types. It does not change how SCTP works. It updates RFC 4960 and was replaced by RFC 9260.

eli5.summary: SCTP sends data in little pieces that carry tiny on-off switches. This sets up an official list so nobody picks the same switch for two different meanings.

questions: how to register sctp chunk flags
what is a sctp chunk flag
how are sctp chunk flags registered
subtitle: A registry for chunk flag assignments in SCTP messages.

tldr.problem: SCTP defines chunk types for different message kinds, and each chunk type needs a way to add flags (on-off switches) for future extensions. The original protocol lacked a formal registration procedure.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6096 creates an IANA registry for chunk flags, where each SCTP chunk type gets its own table of flag values (0x01, 0x02, 0x04, 0x08, 0x10, 0x20, 0x40, 0x80). New flags require an RFC and IANA assignment.
tldr.outcome: Extensions to SCTP can define new flags without conflicts, and the registries document which flags are in use. This RFC was superseded by RFC 9260, which consolidated SCTP specifications.

today: RFC 6096 defined the SCTP chunk flags registry and was updated by RFC 9260, which consolidated all SCTP specifications into a single comprehensive standard. New SCTP extensions now register their chunk flags through RFC 9260.

sections.title: The Problem: Extending SCTP with Flags
sections.content:
SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol) breaks messages into smaller pieces called chunks. Each chunk type (DATA, INIT, SACK, and so on) has a fixed structure defined in RFC 4960, but the protocol needs room for extensions.

RFC 4960 allowed new chunk types to be defined, but did not provide a clear way to add flags to existing chunk types. Since new protocol extensions were being designed that needed flags (for example, to enable optional features), there was a risk that different extensions would assign conflicting meanings to the same flag values.

RFC 6096 solves this by creating a formal registration process, so that flag assignments for each chunk type are coordinated through IANA.
sections.eli5: SCTP chunks are like envelopes, and each envelope type can have little stickers (flags) to mark special information. This RFC makes sure everyone registers their stickers so two people don't use the same sticker to mean different things.

sections.title: Chunk Types and Flags
sections.content:
A chunk in SCTP is a self-describing unit with a type code, flags, length, and value. The chunk type tells the receiver what kind of data it contains: DATA chunks carry application data; INIT and INIT ACK chunks set up connections; SACK chunks acknowledge received data; HEARTBEAT and HEARTBEAT ACK chunks check link health.

Each chunk type has an 8-bit flags field. The standard allows chunk flags to be 0x01, 0x02, 0x04, 0x08, 0x10, 0x20, 0x40, or 0x80—one bit per flag, up to 8 flags per chunk type. An implementation that does not understand a flag sets it to 0 on transmission and ignores it on receipt, so flags are backward compatible.
sections.eli5: A chunk is like a labeled box in an envelope, and the flags are eight tiny on-off switches on the label. Protocols can add new switches without breaking old systems that don't understand them.

sections.title: Registration Procedure
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 4960 with a formal registration procedure. For each SCTP chunk type, IANA maintains a table of which flags are in use and what they mean.

To register a new chunk flag, a document (usually an RFC) MUST specify the chunk type, the flag bit value (0x01 through 0x80), a name for the flag, and a detailed description of what the flag does. The flag value MUST be unique within that chunk type.

Registrations are handled through RFC Required action: only published RFCs can register flags, not informal proposals.
sections.eli5: When someone wants to add a new switch to a chunk type, they write an RFC saying which switch they want and what it does. An official arbiter (IANA) checks that the switch number is not already taken and adds it to the list.

sections.title: Current Registries
sections.content:
RFC 6096 creates registries for chunk types defined in RFC 4960 and related standards. Most registries are initially empty, but a few chunk types already had flags defined:

  • DATA chunk has three flags: E bit (0x01), B bit (0x02), and U bit (0x04), all from RFC 4960.
  • ABORT chunk has the T bit (0x01) from RFC 4960.
  • SHUTDOWN COMPLETE chunk has the T bit (0x01) from RFC 4960.

Other chunk types (INIT, INIT ACK, SACK, HEARTBEAT, HEARTBEAT ACK, ERROR, COOKIE ECHO, COOKIE ACK, ECNE, CWR, AUTH, ASCONF ACK, PAD, FORWARD TSN, and ASCONF) start with empty flag registries, available for future extensions.
sections.eli5: The DATA chunk already has three switches defined. Most other chunk types don't have any yet, so they have room to add switches in the future.

sections.title: Security Impact
sections.content:
RFC 6096 itself does not change SCTP's security. The registry only documents which flags are allocated, and the registration procedure ensures that extensions go through public review.

The underlying SCTP specification RFC 4960 handles security and privacy. Future extensions that define new flags must provide their own security analysis in the RFC that registers them.
sections.eli5: This RFC just keeps track of which stickers are used and makes sure new stickers are documented. The actual safety of SCTP messages is handled elsewhere.
